title: Cytochrome c: a real protein tree

source.citation: UniProt Consortium, UniProtKB (uniprot.org); aligned with MAFFT v7.525

prompts.concept: This is real data: cytochrome c, a ~110-site protein found in almost every eukaryote, from eight species spanning the deepest splits in the tree of life — human, horse, chicken, zebrafish, Drosophila, wheat, yeast and Neurospora. The sequences come from UniProt (CC BY 4.0) and were aligned with MAFFT; the reference panel shows the accepted classification, not a known true tree.
prompts.math: Cytochrome c is small and ancient: even the deepest pair (Drosophila–Neurospora) carries a JTT distance of only ~0.74 substitutions per site — long, but well below the saturation ceiling.

prompts.concept: The matrix shows JTT-corrected distances. The smallest cell is horse–chicken at 0.119 — yet that pair will not join first, because NJ scores pairs by Q, which also counts how far each lineage is from everything else. Which two species join first?
prompts.math: NJ joins the pair minimizing Q(i,j) = (n−2)·d(i,j) − R_i − R_j. The two fungi sit far from every animal and plant — their large row sums R pull their Q below every other pair's.
prompts.reveal: The two fungi join first: yeast–Neurospora at 0.464 wins on Q even though it is nowhere near the smallest distance. Click the horse–chicken cell to open "How was this distance computed?": at 0.119 it is the matrix minimum, but each vertebrate stays close to all the others, so their pair scores worse on Q.

prompts.concept: Two joins in, the deepest divide is already visible: the fungi paired, wheat attached to them, and now the insect joins that side. Nothing here says wheat is a fungus — in an unrooted tree, "plants and fungi" versus "animals" is simply the deepest split, and NJ found it from the far end.
prompts.math: A tree read as unrooted has no direction: a leaf grafted near an outgroup root marks where the ingroup/outgroup edge sits, not which side is older.

prompts.concept: Only the vertebrates are left on the animal side — and look at the matrix: every distance among human, horse, chicken and zebrafish is 0.10–0.18, a tiny corner compared to the 0.4–0.7 separating the big groups. The last joins order these four, and this is exactly where a short protein is weakest.
prompts.math: Within-vertebrate distances run 0.10–0.18 while animal-to-fungus runs 0.4–0.7. The tree has plenty of signal for the old splits and very little for the young ones.

prompts.concept: The tree is complete, and it differs from the accepted classification in only 1 clade. The big divisions are all right: fungi together, plant-and-fungi versus animals, vertebrates together, mammals together. The single miss is inside the vertebrates — chicken pairs with zebrafish instead of sitting next to the mammals. That is the honest limit of one short, slowly evolving protein: 110 conserved sites resolve billion-year-old splits but cannot reliably order four vertebrates that are all less than 0.2 apart.
prompts.math: RF counts clades present in one tree but not the other. Here the missing clade is {chicken, mammals}: the inferred tree substitutes the equally short alternative {chicken, zebrafish}.
